items.text: Elicits the site of onset and migration of the pain, and anorexia, nausea or vomiting
Directs an abdominal examination for right lower quadrant tenderness, rebound or guarding, with step-by-step instructions
Obtains temperature and heart rate within the first hour
Uses ultrasound to assess the right lower quadrant or to look for an alternative cause
Evaluates for urolithiasis or a urinary tract cause, e.g. with a urine dipstick
Initiates an antibiotic regimen from the kit with enteric gram-negative and anaerobic coverage
Elicits the nature of the penicillin reaction, or selects a regimen without beta-lactam cross-reactivity and states why
Plans the full antibiotic course within kit stock, including IV-to-oral step-down
Sets a reassessment interval and names signs of deterioration (fever, abdominal rigidity, rising heart rate)
Consults ground support allowing for the communication delay, and continues care while sheltered
Explains the risk of perforation and the plan if it occurs
Explanation of the plan to a non-physician CMO

anchors.1: Unexplained jargon, or instructions the CMO could not follow
anchors.3: Clear plan; the CMO's understanding not confirmed
anchors.5: Plain step-by-step instructions, closed-loop confirmation, and explicit monitoring and call-back criteria

items.text: Recommends removal to definitive care once signs of peritonitis appear
Stops the penicillin and gives an antihistamine from the kit
Directs the crew to operate (appendectomy or any incision)
Includes CT imaging or evacuation to Earth in the plan
Commits to food poisoning or gastroenteritis without re-examining the abdomen
Recommends ceftriaxone or another beta-lactam without eliciting the nature of the penicillin reaction

notes: Worked example. Diagnosis and etiology are scored by the standard items SDX and SET. Weights are illustrative until the clinical lead calibrates them.
